title: How Does AI Pick the Next Word? The Real Scores Inside a Local AI (Qwen 3.5)

thumb.headline:
HOW AI PICKS
THE NEXT WORD

beats.narration: Once upon a time, there was a... what comes next? The AI does not know yet. First it gives a score to every chip it could write next. Then it picks one, adds it to the sentence, and does the whole thing again. That loop is how an AI writes.

beats.narration: These are the real scores, from a small AI called Qwen, running on my laptop. The top one, young, gets about thirty percent. Little and curious come next. Here it picks the top one, young, and adds it to the sentence.

beats.narration: A chip, or token, is a piece of text the AI reads and writes. Here each one is a whole word with its space in front: that dot marks the space. Sometimes a chip is only part of a word, or a full stop. And the AI scores every chip it knows, about two hundred forty-eight thousand of them, all at once. The top five shown here add up to about seventy-five percent. Everything else it knows shares the rest.

beats.narration: Now watch the loop. Here it always takes the top score. With young in the sentence, every score changes: now adventurer, boy and student lead. Adventurer wins with about twenty-one percent. In the next round, named gets ninety-nine point seven percent: almost certain. Then a name: Lily, ahead of Alex. Then a full stop. Five rounds, five chips, one sentence. Each round adds just one chip.

beats.narration: But an AI app usually does not take the top score every time. It draws one chip at random, and a higher score only means a better chance. So I switched off the extra filters and let it draw the first chip a hundred times, straight from these scores. Young came out thirty times. Curious came out twenty times, more than little this time, just by chance. In total, twenty-six different words came out: the top five, plus twenty-one others, like furry and retired. The scores stay the same. The draw is what changes.

beats.narration: If you write code, you can see these scores yourself. These eight lines of Python ask Ollama for one chip, with log probs turned on, and the top five. Each score comes back as a log prob, and math dot exp, times a hundred, turns it into a percent. Run it, and young comes back with twenty-nine point six percent, the same score we saw before.

beats.narration: So an AI writes one chip at a time. It scores every chip it knows, picks one, adds it to the sentence, and repeats, until the answer is done. These scores come from one small model on my laptop. A different model would likely give different scores, but the loop is the same.
